name: Cheadle Hulme School
text: Your train passes near Cheadle Hulme School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1855 as the Manchester Warehousemen and Clerks' Orphan Schools. It moved here from Ardwick in 1869, and its grounds now cover 83 acres.

name: Handforth Hall
text: Your train passes near Handforth Hall, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed manor house built by Sir Urian Brereton and dated 1562 in a carved inscription by its porch. It was once the home of Sir William Brereton, a Parliamentary commander in the Civil War.

name: Edgeley Park
text: Your train passes near Edgeley Park, on the train's {side}, built in 1891 for a rugby league club and home to Stockport County since 1902. When frost made Maine Road's pitch unplayable in January 1958, England played two training matches here on the same day.

name: Baguley Hall
text: Your train passes near Baguley Hall, on the train's {side}, built in the early 14th century by Sir William de Baguley and one of the oldest surviving timber great halls in England. During the Second World War it was a farm, known locally as Maher's Farm.

name: Old Town Hall, Altrincham
text: Your train passes near Altrincham's Old Town Hall, on the train's {side}, completed in 1849 for the Earl of Stamford, whose country seat was Dunham Massey Hall. The old borough's court leet met in its first-floor council chamber until the court was abolished in 1883.

name: Altrincham Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Altrincham Town Hall, on the train's {side}, built in red brick in the Jacobean style and opened in November 1901. Building work was held up while the builder removed an uncharted water cistern from the site.

name: Ashley Hall
text: Your train passes near Ashley Hall, on the train's {side}, where Cheshire's gentlemen met in 1715 to decide whether to support the Stuarts or the Hanoverians. They chose the Hanoverians, and the portraits they later commissioned now hang in Tatton Hall.

name: St Elizabeth's Church, Ashley
text: Your train passes near St Elizabeth's Church, Ashley, on the train's {side}, built of red brick and red terracotta in 1880 to a design by Wilbraham Egerton, later the first Earl Egerton. Its organ, built in 1885, was first made for a house.

name: Brook Street Chapel
text: Your train passes near Brook Street Chapel, on the train's {side}, a Unitarian chapel built soon after the Toleration Act 1688 and still in use. The novelist Elizabeth Gaskell, who died in 1865, is buried here, with her husband William.

name: Gaskell Memorial Tower and King's Coffee House
text: Your train passes near the Gaskell Memorial Tower and King's Coffee House, on the train's {side}, opened in 1907 as council offices, a coffee house and a memorial to Elizabeth Gaskell, whose novel Cranford drew on the town. Its designer, Richard Harding Watt, hoped the coffee house would draw people away from the inns.

name: Holford Hall
text: Your train passes near Holford Hall, on the train's {side}, a fragment of a much larger timber-framed house built in 1601 for Mary Cholmondeley on a moated site. Part of the house was pulled down in the 1880s, and the moated site is a scheduled monument.

name: St Helen Witton Church
text: Your train passes near St Helen's, Witton, on the train's {side}, Northwich's parish church, which Alec Clifton-Taylor counted among England's best parish churches. Its tower was built in about 1498 by a mason named Thomas Hunter, whose name is displayed on it.

name: Weaver Hall Museum and Workhouse
text: Your train passes near the Weaver Hall Museum and Workhouse, on the train's {side}, a museum of West Cheshire's history in the old Northwich Union Workhouse of 1839. It was once the Salt Museum, after the industry that made the town the salt capital of the world.

name: Torr Vale Mill
text: Your train passes near Torr Vale Mill, on the train's {side}, a cotton mill built in the late 1780s at the bottom of the Torrs gorge in New Mills. It made towelling until December 2000, the UK's longest continuous period of cotton production, and appeared on Royal Mail stamps that year.

name: Stockport School
text: Your train passes near Stockport School, on the train's {side}, which began in 1888 as a technical school, proposed to mark the 50th anniversary of Queen Victoria's reign. It opened to day pupils in 1896 and moved to its present site in 1938.

name: Stockport Grammar School
text: Your train passes near Stockport Grammar School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1487 by Sir Edmund Shaa, a former Lord Mayor of London. Shaa's will provided for a school and a chapel in St Mary's Church, and the school moved to its present site in 1915.

name: Stockport War Memorial Art Gallery
text: Your train passes near the Stockport War Memorial Art Gallery, on the train's {side}, built in Portland stone as the town's main memorial to those who died in the First World War. Paid for entirely by voluntary subscriptions, it was opened by Prince Henry in October 1925.

name: Stockport Viaduct
text: Your train crosses Stockport Viaduct over the Mersey valley, completed in December 1840 for the Manchester and Birmingham Railway. About 11 million bricks went into it, and when it was finished it was the world's largest viaduct.

name: National Aircraft Factory No. 2
text: Your train passes near the site of National Aircraft Factory No. 2, on the train's {side}, a First World War government factory beside the line that built 444 DH.9 bombers in 1918 and 1919. Fairey Aviation bought it in 1934 and built aircraft there until the late 1950s.

name: Hyde Road
text: Your train passes near the site of Hyde Road, on the train's {side}, Manchester City's ground from 1887 until 1923. Its players changed in a nearby pub until 1896, and a section of its roof, sold to The Shay in Halifax, is still in use there.

name: Hat Works
text: Your train passes near the Hat Works, on the train's {side}, a museum of hatting in Wellington Mill. The mill was built in 1830 and 1831 as an early fireproof cotton-spinning mill, and became a hat works in the 1890s.

name: St Elisabeth's Church, Reddish
text: Your train passes near St Elisabeth's Church, on the train's {side}, designed by Alfred Waterhouse and paid for by the mill owner Sir William Houldsworth, who named it after his wife. Pillars for its nave were carried from the nearby canal by elephants from Belle Vue Zoo.

name: Audenshaw Reservoirs
text: Your train passes near the Audenshaw Reservoirs, on the train's {side}, three reservoirs built for Manchester Corporation between 1877 and 1882 under John Frederick Bateman. Part of Audenshaw village was demolished to make way for them.

name: Ryecroft Hall
text: Your train passes near Ryecroft Hall, on the train's {side}, a mill owner's house that Austin Hopkinson bought in 1913 and later gave to the people of Audenshaw. During the First World War it was a voluntary hospital with more than 100 beds.

name: Fairfield Moravian Settlement
text: Your train passes near the Fairfield Moravian Settlement, on the train's {side}, founded in 1785 by Benjamin La Trobe as a centre for the Moravian Church's work around Manchester. Building it cost £6,000, with money from Moravian congregations in England, Germany and America.

name: Gorton Monastery
text: Your train passes near Gorton Monastery, on the train's {side}, a Franciscan friary church designed by Edward Welby Pugin and built between 1866 and 1872. Stripped and left derelict after it closed in 1989, it reopened in 2007 as an events venue and heritage space.

name: Belle Vue Zoological Gardens
text: Your train passes near the site of Belle Vue Zoological Gardens, on the train's {side}, opened in 1836, whose zoo grew to be the third largest in the United Kingdom. At its peak it drew more than two million visitors a year; the zoo closed in 1977.

name: Bradford Colliery
text: Your train passes near the site of Bradford Colliery, on the train's {side}, where coal was mined from at least the early 17th century. Subsidence made it uneconomic despite its large reserves of good coal, and it closed in 1968; the site is now under the City of Manchester Stadium.

name: Co-op Live
text: Your train passes near Co-op Live, on the train's {side}, which opened on 14 May 2024 as the largest indoor arena in the United Kingdom, holding 23,500 people. The Bury band Elbow officially opened it.

name: Broadhurst Park
text: Your train passes near Broadhurst Park, on the train's {side}, home of FC United of Manchester, a fan-owned club formed in 2005 by Manchester United supporters after the Glazer takeover. The ground opened in May 2015 with a friendly against Benfica B.

name: Foxdenton Hall
text: Your train passes near Foxdenton Hall, on the train's {side}, a Georgian house built between 1710 and 1730 for Alexander Radclyffe on the base of an earlier hall of 1620. In 1922 the family leased the hall and its park to Chadderton Council, which opened them to the public.

name: Elm Street School
text: Your train passes near Elm Street School, on the train's {side}, built between 1908 and 1910 to designs by Edgar Wood and J. Henry Sellers, and a landmark of Arts and Crafts and Modernism. Still a primary school, it is now called Elm Wood in Wood's honour.

name: St John the Baptist Church, Rochdale
text: Your train passes near St John the Baptist Church, on the train's {side}, a Catholic church in the Byzantine Revival style, completed in 1927. Its parish priest, Canon Henry Chipp, wanted it to resemble Hagia Sophia in Istanbul.

name: St Chad's Church, Rochdale
text: Your train passes near St Chad's Church, on the train's {side}, Rochdale's parish church, founded before 1170 and reached from the town below by a flight of 124 steps. A local legend says spirits and fairies chose its hilltop site by moving the building stone up from near the river.

name: Stubley Old Hall
text: Your train passes near Stubley Old Hall, on the train's {side}, a manor house parts of which are thought to date from the 15th century. Its oldest part, the south wing, is cruck-framed, and its front was faced in stone around 1600.

name: Summit Tunnel
text: Your train goes through Summit Tunnel, built under the Pennines between 1838 and 1841 for the Manchester and Leeds Railway. When it opened it was the longest railway tunnel in the world, and it carries both tracks in a single horseshoe-shaped tube.

name: Ashton-under-Lyne War Memorial
text: Your train passes near Ashton-under-Lyne War Memorial, on the train's {side}, unveiled in 1922 by General Sir Ian Hamilton; the town lost more than 1,500 men in the First World War. Winged Victory stands at its top, and two bronze lions flank its base.

name: St Michael and All Angels' Church, Ashton-under-Lyne
text: Your train passes near St Michael and All Angels' Church, on the train's {side}, which stood by 1262 and was rebuilt in the 15th century by Sir John Assheton. Its tower, rebuilt in 1886 to 1888, is modelled on that of Manchester Cathedral.

name: Old Hall Chapel
text: Your train passes near Old Hall Chapel, on the train's {side}, built in the late 16th or early 17th century as the Dukinfield family's chapel. Samuel Eaton set up a Congregational church here in about 1640, described as the first Independent church set up in England.
